one_liner: DuckDB extension that runs DuckDB's SQL plans on NVIDIA GPUs via libcudf; vendor TPC-H hot runs 2.7-5.7x faster than DuckDB.
what_it_does: Sirius is a C++20/CUDA engine loaded into DuckDB as an extension; once loaded, optimizer hooks capture DuckDB's optimized logical plan and run it on the GPU, so the SQL, DuckDB shell and Python API stay the same with no query rewrites (`SET gpu_execution = false` turns it off). It reads Parquet (local through io_uring, or from S3) and file-backed DuckDB tables. `CALL pin_table(...)` caches columns in GPU memory or pinned host memory for hot runs. Plans with an unsupported operator or type fall back to DuckDB's CPU engine without telling you.
how_it_is_fast: It runs columnar operators on the GPU at HBM bandwidth using libcudf primitives: cuDF hash join and groupby, sort, and cuDF AST or NVRTC-JIT expression evaluation (`cudf::compute_column_jit`). The current "Super Sirius" engine is task-based and pipelined. It uses cuCascade tiered memory (GPU, then pinned host, then disk), adaptive hash partitioning, spilling and a 3-phase sample/partition/merge sort, so inputs can be larger than GPU memory. Scans get less data through dynamic filters built on the hash-join build side (Bloom, cuco IN-list set, zone maps), Parquet row-group pruning, io_uring O_DIRECT reads with a prefetch cache, and optional Simpatico-compressed pinned tables (for example delta->bitpack) that skip file I/O and decode on hot runs.
when_to_use: Repeated (hot) analytical SQL, i.e. TPC-H-style multi-way joins plus group-by, over 100 GB-1 TB of Parquet or file-backed DuckDB, with the hot tables pinned in GPU or pinned-host memory
You already run DuckDB and have a Linux box with an NVIDIA Turing-or-newer GPU. You want existing SQL to run faster without rewrites, and you accept that unsupported queries keep working on the CPU
Cost per query matters more than raw box size: the vendor chart shows 2.1-5.3x lower cost per TPC-H run on AWS g7e (RTX PRO 6000) than DuckDB on a Graviton5 m9g.16xlarge
Data sits on local NVMe that supports O_DIRECT, so the io_uring scan path and prefetch cache can feed the GPU
GPU query-processing research: operators can be swapped between libcudf and hand-written CUDA kernels, and DuckDB serves as a built-in CPU baseline
when_not_to_use: Cold or one-shot queries. Data still reaches the GPU through a CPU-mediated scan. In ClickBench (March 2026, legacy path, p5.4xlarge) Sirius's cold-run sum was 977.9s against DuckDB's 161.5s on c8g.metal-48xl, even though its hot-run sum was 1.50s against 11.29s. CUDA/cuDF startup can take minutes, and the first NVRTC JIT pass cost about 19s on the SF1000 run

Queries built around window functions, ASOF JOIN, nested types (STRUCT/variable LIST), HUGEINT/128-bit types, BIGINT SUM or BIGINT arithmetic (no INT128 accumulator). These fall back and run at plain DuckDB CPU speed
In-memory DuckDB databases (`:memory:` tables): the native scan requires a single-file block manager, so these queries fall back to the CPU

Correctness-critical production use without your own GPU-vs-CPU validation. Wrong-result bugs are open: #1452 (pinned table + ORDER BY over a decimal expression races and silently duplicates and drops rows), #1312 (prefetch cache + multiple GPUs returns wrong sums) and #1123 (latent join-filter pushdown below LIMIT/TOP_N inherited from the pinned DuckDB)

No NVIDIA GPU, or macOS/Windows, or containers that block the io_uring syscalls. The advantage also shrinks as data outgrows GPU memory (5.5x at SF100 down to 2.7x at SF1000 in the vendor chart), and the tuned SF1000 repro used 251.7 of 256 GB of GPU memory plus about 470 GB of host RAM

integration.form: shared lib (loadable, unsigned `sirius.duckdb_extension`, or statically built into a bundled `duckdb` binary); source build only, with no tagged releases or prebuilt binaries
integration.dependencies: libcudf 26.08.01 (RAPIDS), RMM, NVIDIA cuCascade, CUDA toolkit + NVRTC, a patched DuckDB 1.5.5 fork (sirius-db/duckdb v1.5.5-patches), liburing, yaml-cpp, abseil, spdlog 1.8, CRoaring, protobuf and a Rust toolchain, all managed through Pixi
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 / CUDA C++20, CMake >= 3.30.4 (Pixi pins 4.x), conda GCC or Clang 21; CUDA 12.x (driver >= 525.60.13) or CUDA 13.x (driver >= 580.65.06)
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 or aarch64 with glibc >= 2.28; NVIDIA GPU of compute capability 7.5+ (Turing or newer); io_uring enabled at runtime; no macOS/Windows engine build
integration.thread_safety: Each DuckDB connection gets a SiriusContext that owns the engine's thread pools and memory tiers. The vendor ran a 7-stream TPC-H throughput test, but the project lists multi-query GPU memory isolation and admission control as open problems. Guarantees are otherwise not documented.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — after LOAD you use the same DuckDB SQL, CLI and Python API with no query rewrites. However, it needs a Sirius-built DuckDB 1.5.5 (patched fork, unsigned extension), and unsupported operators or types silently run on DuckDB's CPU engine

gotchas: Fallback is silent by default. Set `enable_duckdb_fallback = false` to surface errors. The scan docs say a runtime (not plan-time) fallback can poison the connection so that the next GPU query on it deadlocks, and S3 scans have no CPU fallback at all.

Hot-run speed depends on `pin_table`, because Sirius otherwise re-reads storage on every query. Pinned DuckDB tables reject UPDATE, MERGE ... UPDATE and ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, and an explicit CHECKPOINT invalidates the pin until you re-pin.

Defaults take 95% of GPU memory plus 8 GiB of pinned host memory per NUMA node, and use the interpreted AST expression evaluator. The SF1000 repro found `SET expression_evaluator_strategy = 'ast_jit'` 4.17% faster, but it is not the default. A pre-optimizer hook also disables some DuckDB optimizers (IN_CLAUSE, COMPRESSED_MATERIALIZATION, LATE_MATERIALIZATION), and plans still come from DuckDB's CPU cost model.

The README and the CIDR'26 paper describe integration through Substrait, but the current DuckDB path consumes DuckDB's logical plan through optimizer hooks (the Substrait include is commented out in sirius_extension.cpp). The ClickBench entry was run with the legacy in-memory `gpu_processing` path, which is no longer built by default.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Sirius over cuDF (cudf.pandas) when the workload is SQL over DuckDB tables or Parquet, with large joins that may exceed GPU memory, rather than pandas code. Pick it over the CPU engines (Umbra, chDB, Velox-based Prestissimo) only when you have an NVIDIA GPU and repeated hot queries on pinned data; for cold scans, or with no GPU, those CPU engines are the safer choice.
verified_claims_summary: The README chart (first-party) gives TPC-H 22-query hot-run totals for Sirius on the best of AWS g7e.2xlarge/4xlarge/8xlarge (RTX PRO 6000 96 GB) against DuckDB v1.5.5 on a Graviton5 m9g.16xlarge: 1.71s vs 9.37s at SF100 (5.5x), 4.48s vs 25.72s at SF300, 8.14s vs 42.25s at SF500 and 31.79s vs 85.91s at SF1000 (2.7x), with 2.1-5.3x lower cost per run. The chart states no compiler flags, per-SF instance, config or pinning setup, and the comparison is across hardware; independent ClickBench data (March 2026, p5.4xlarge, legacy path) shows a 1.50s hot sum against DuckDB's 11.29s on c8g.metal-48xl, but a far slower cold run.
status_note: Actively developed by NVIDIA, UW-Madison and about 40 contributors (last commit 2026-09-24, ~150 open issues) under Apache-2.0, but it has no releases (CMake version 0.0.0), so expect to build from source with Pixi against pinned libcudf 26.08.01 and a patched DuckDB 1.5.5, and to track fast-moving internals.
